## Overview

Latent change score models describe change itself
[@McArdle-2009].
Take vocabulary and reading comprehension measured once a year in children.
From one occasion to the next, each child's vocabulary changes.
In the dual change score model, the change has two sources:
a constant amount each child gains every year (the slope),
and an amount that depends on where the child stood the year before
(the self-feedback).
In the bivariate model, the change in one variable
can also depend on the previous level of the other variable
(the coupling),
for example, if children with a larger vocabulary
gain more in reading comprehension.

The dual change score model is usually fitted
as a structural equation model (SEM).
It can also be written as a state space model:
the true levels of the two variables are latent states,
and the slopes are latent states that never change.

This tutorial does three things:

1. It writes the bivariate dual change score model as a state space model.
2. It simulates data from the model with `SimSSMFixed()`.
3. It fits the model to the simulated data
   as a state space model with `dynr` and `OpenMx`
   and as a structural equation model (SEM) with `lavaan` and `OpenMx`,
   and compares every set of estimates with the values used to simulate the data.

No prior knowledge of state space models is needed.



## Model

The measurement model is given by
$$
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    Y_{1_{i, t}} \\
    Y_{2_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  =
  \left(
  \begin{array}{cccc}
    1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
    0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \eta_{1_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{2_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{3_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{4_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  +
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \varepsilon_{1_{i, t}} \\
    \varepsilon_{2_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right),
  \quad
  \mathrm{with}
  \quad
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \varepsilon_{1_{i, t}} \\
    \varepsilon_{2_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \sim
  \mathcal{N}
  \left(
  \mathbf{0},
  \left(
  \begin{array}{cc}
    \theta_{11} & 0 \\
    0 & \theta_{22} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \right)
$$
where $Y_{1_{i, t}}$ and $Y_{2_{i, t}}$
are the two observed variables
at time $t$ and individual $i$,
$\eta_{1_{i, t}}$ and $\eta_{2_{i, t}}$ are their true levels,
$\eta_{3_{i, t}}$ and $\eta_{4_{i, t}}$ are their slopes,
and $\theta_{11}$ and $\theta_{22}$
are the measurement error variances.

In words,
each observed score is the true level plus measurement error.
The slopes have loadings of 0:
they affect the scores only through the change in the true levels.

The change in the true level of the first variable
from occasion $t - 1$ to occasion $t$ is
$$
  \Delta \eta_{1_{i, t}}
  =
  \eta_{3_{i, t - 1}}
  +
  b_{1} \eta_{1_{i, t - 1}}
  +
  g_{12} \eta_{2_{i, t - 1}} ,
$$
and similarly for the second variable,
$\Delta \eta_{2_{i, t}} = \eta_{4_{i, t - 1}} + b_{2} \eta_{2_{i, t - 1}} + g_{21} \eta_{1_{i, t - 1}}$.
The true level at occasion $t$ is the previous true level plus the change,
$\eta_{1_{i, t}} = \eta_{1_{i, t - 1}} + \Delta \eta_{1_{i, t}}$.

Writing the change into the level gives the dynamic structure
$$
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \eta_{1_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{2_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{3_{i, t}} \\
    \eta_{4_{i, t}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  =
  \left(
  \begin{array}{cccc}
    1 + b_{1} & g_{12} & 1 & 0 \\
    g_{21} & 1 + b_{2} & 0 & 1 \\
    0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
    0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \eta_{1_{i, t - 1}} \\
    \eta_{2_{i, t - 1}} \\
    \eta_{3_{i, t - 1}} \\
    \eta_{4_{i, t - 1}} \\
  \end{array}
  \right) .
$$

In words,
$b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$ are the self-feedback effects:
a negative value means that individuals who stand higher
gain less, so the levels level off over time.
$g_{12}$ is the coupling from the second variable to the first:
a positive value means that a higher level of the second variable
is followed by a larger gain in the first.
$g_{21}$ is the reverse.
The slopes stay the same over time.
As in most applications of the model,
there is no process noise:
once the initial levels and the slopes are set,
the true trajectories are fixed.

The initial condition holds the means, variances, and covariances
of the initial true levels and the slopes,
$$
  \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, 0}
  \sim
  \mathcal{N}
  \left(
  \boldsymbol{\mu}_{0},
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}
  \right) .
$$

For example, a positive covariance between the initial level
and the slope of the same variable means that individuals who start higher
also tend to gain more each year.

### Diagrams



![Path diagram of the dual change score model.](fig-vignettes-lcs-path.png){width=100%}

The bivariate dual change score model as a path diagram, for the first three occasions ($t = 0, 1, 2$).
The true level at each occasion, $\eta_{1}$ or $\eta_{2}$, is the previous level plus the latent change $\Delta \eta_{1}$ or $\Delta \eta_{2}$ (the arrows with a loading of 1).
Each change is the slope ($\eta_{3}$ or $\eta_{4}$), plus the self-feedback effect ($b_{1}$ or $b_{2}$) of the previous level of the same variable, plus the coupling effect ($g_{12}$ or $g_{21}$) of the previous level of the other variable.
$\varepsilon_{1}$ and $\varepsilon_{2}$ are the measurement errors, with variances $\theta_{11}$ and $\theta_{22}$.
A loop on a variable is its variance and a curved two-headed arrow a covariance.
The initial levels and the slopes have variances $\sigma_{11}$ to $\sigma_{44}$ and all covary; to keep the diagram readable, only the covariances $\sigma_{12}$, $\sigma_{13}$, $\sigma_{24}$, and $\sigma_{34}$ are drawn.

![State space form of the dual change score model.](fig-vignettes-lcs-ssm.png){width=100%}

The same model in state space form, for the first three occasions, with every element of the state drawn.
The latent changes are not states: writing each change into the level gives the arrows $1 + b_{1}$, $1 + b_{2}$, $g_{12}$, and $g_{21}$ between the levels $\eta_{1, t}$ and $\eta_{2, t}$, and the arrows with a loading of 1 from the slopes.
The slopes are states with a transition of 1, so $\eta_{3, t} = \eta_{3}$ and $\eta_{4, t} = \eta_{4}$ for all $t$.
There is no process noise.
At $t = 0$, the initial condition $\boldsymbol{\eta}_{0} \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}_{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} \right)$ gives all the variances and covariances of the levels and the slopes at $t = 0$.
Below the diagram, all the latent variables at one occasion form the state vector $\boldsymbol{\eta}_{t}$, and all the observed variables form $\mathbf{y}_{t}$:
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ carries the state from one occasion to the next, $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ maps the state to the observed variables, and $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ is the covariance matrix of the measurement error $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t}$.
`SimSSMFixed()` takes `beta`, `lambda`, `mu0`, and the Cholesky factors of $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}$ (`theta_l` and `sigma0_l`);
`psi_l` is a matrix of zeros.

## Data Generation

### Notation

Let $t = 6$ be the number of time points and $n = 2000$ be the number of individuals.

Let the self-feedback effects be $b_{1} = -0.2$ and $b_{2} = -0.3$,
and the coupling effects be $g_{12} = 0.1$ and $g_{21} = 0.2$,
so that

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}
=
\left(
\begin{array}{cccc}
  0.8 & 0.1 & 1 & 0 \\
  0.2 & 0.7 & 0 & 1 \\
  0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
  0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
\end{array}
\right) .
$$

Let the initial condition be

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{0}
=
\left(
\begin{array}{c}
  2 \\
  1 \\
  0.5 \\
  0.4 \\
\end{array}
\right)
\quad \mathrm{and,} \quad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}
=
\left(
\begin{array}{cccc}
  1 & 0.3 & 0.15 & 0.05 \\
  0.3 & 1 & 0.05 & 0.15 \\
  0.15 & 0.05 & 0.25 & 0.05 \\
  0.05 & 0.15 & 0.05 & 0.25 \\
\end{array}
\right) ,
$$

and the measurement error variances be
$\theta_{11} = 0.2$ and $\theta_{22} = 0.2$.

### R Function Arguments

The simulation functions take covariance matrices
as lower triangular Cholesky factors (the arguments ending in `_l`).
There is no process noise, so `psi` and `psi_l` are zero matrices.


``` r

time

mu0

sigma0

#> [4,] 0.05 0.15 0.05 0.25
sigma0_l # sigma0_l <- t(chol(sigma0))
```

### Visualizing the Dynamics Without Measurement Error (n = 5 with Different Initial Condition)

Without measurement error,
each individual's true levels follow smooth curves
that bend as the self-feedback slows the gains.

### Using the `SimSSMFixed` Function from the `simStateSpace` Package to Simulate Data

Now we add the measurement error and simulate the full data set.
`as.data.frame()` returns the data in long format,
one row per individual and time point,
with the columns `id`, `time`, `y1`, and `y2`.


``` r
library(simStateSpace)
sim <- SimSSMFixed(
  n = n,
  time = time,
  mu0 = mu0,
  sigma0_l = sigma0_l,
  alpha = alpha,
  beta = beta,
  psi_l = psi_l,
  nu = nu,
  lambda = lambda,
  theta_l = theta_l,
  type = 0
)
data <- as.data.frame(sim)
head(data)
#>   id time       y1           y2
#> 1  1    0 1.239124 -0.034741096
#> 2  1    1 2.372287 -0.050275519
#> 3  1    2 2.550748 -0.363167146
#> 4  1    3 3.417814 -0.164406246
#> 5  1    4 3.685087  0.007406512
#> 6  1    5 3.473986 -0.348501993
summary(data)
#>        id              time           y1               y2         
#>  Min.   :   1.0   Min.   :0.0   Min.   :-4.200   Min.   :-5.4249  
#>  1st Qu.: 500.8   1st Qu.:1.0   1st Qu.: 1.429   1st Qu.: 0.8064  
#>  Median :1000.5   Median :2.5   Median : 2.446   Median : 1.8475  
#>  Mean   :1000.5   Mean   :2.5   Mean   : 2.515   Mean   : 1.9371  
#>  3rd Qu.:1500.2   3rd Qu.:4.0   3rd Qu.: 3.516   3rd Qu.: 2.9450  
#>  Max.   :2000.0   Max.   :5.0   Max.   : 9.998   Max.   : 8.7711
plot(sim)
```

## Model Fitting

The same simulated data are fitted
as a state space model with `dynr` and `OpenMx`
and as a structural equation model (SEM) with `lavaan` and `OpenMx`.
All of them estimate the parameters by maximum likelihood.
The section Population Values and Estimates
compares their estimates with the population values.

### dynr

We fit the model with `dynr`,
which estimates state space models by maximum likelihood
using the Kalman filter.

A `dynr` model is built from pieces that match the equations above:
the data, the initial condition, the measurement model,
the dynamic model, and the noise.
Each parameter gets a name (for example, `g_1_2` for $g_{12}$),
and the same name used in two places means one shared parameter.
The starting values are set to the population values for convenience;
with real data, they would be rough guesses.

#### Prepare Data

Tell `dynr` which columns hold the individual, the time, and the observed variables.


``` r
dynr_data <- dynr::dynr.data(
  dataframe = data,
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  observed = c("y1", "y2")
)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'car':
#>   method           from
#>   na.action.merMod lme4
```

#### Prepare Initial Condition

The means, variances, and covariances
of the initial true levels and the slopes are all estimated.


``` r
dynr_initial <- dynr::prep.initial(
  values.inistate = mu0,
  params.inistate = c("mu0_1_1", "mu0_2_1", "mu0_3_1", "mu0_4_1"),
  values.inicov = sigma0,
  params.inicov = matrix(
    data = c(
      "sigma0_1_1", "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_3_1", "sigma0_4_1",
      "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_2_2", "sigma0_3_2", "sigma0_4_2",
      "sigma0_3_1", "sigma0_3_2", "sigma0_3_3", "sigma0_4_3",
      "sigma0_4_1", "sigma0_4_2", "sigma0_4_3", "sigma0_4_4"
    ),
    nrow = 4
  )
)
```

#### Prepare Measurement Model

The loadings are fixed.


``` r
dynr_measurement <- dynr::prep.measurement(
  values.load = lambda,
  params.load = matrix(data = "fixed", nrow = 2, ncol = 4),
  state.names = c("eta_1", "eta_2", "eta_3", "eta_4"),
  obs.names = c("y1", "y2")
)
```

#### Prepare Dynamic Process

The first two formulas read as
"the new true level is the previous level plus the change",
with the change made of the slope, the self-feedback, and the coupling.
The slopes carry over unchanged.


``` r
dynr_dynamics <- dynr::prep.formulaDynamics(
  formula = list(
    eta_1 ~ eta_1 + eta_3 + b_1 * eta_1 + g_1_2 * eta_2,
    eta_2 ~ eta_2 + eta_4 + b_2 * eta_2 + g_2_1 * eta_1,
    eta_3 ~ eta_3,
    eta_4 ~ eta_4
  ),
  startval = c(
    b_1 = b_1, b_2 = b_2,
    g_1_2 = g_1_2, g_2_1 = g_2_1
  ),
  isContinuousTime = FALSE
)
```

#### Prepare Process Noise

The process noise is fixed at zero,
and the two measurement error variances are estimated.


``` r
dynr_noise <- dynr::prep.noise(
  values.latent = psi,
  params.latent = matrix(data = "fixed", nrow = 4, ncol = 4),
  values.observed = theta,
  params.observed = matrix(
    data = c(
      "theta_1_1", "fixed",
      "fixed", "theta_2_2"
    ),
    nrow = 2
  )
)
```

#### Prepare the Model

The pieces are put together into one model.
`dynr` writes the model as C code to `outfile` and compiles it.


``` r
model <- dynr::dynr.model(
  data = dynr_data,
  initial = dynr_initial,
  measurement = dynr_measurement,
  dynamics = dynr_dynamics,
  noise = dynr_noise,
  outfile = "lcs.c"
)
```

The plot below shows the model equations with the parameter names.

<img src="fig-vignettes-lcs-model-lcs-1.png" alt="" width="3300" />

#### Fit the Model


``` r
results <- dynr::dynr.cook(
  model,
  debug_flag = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

### OpenMx: State Space Model

`OpenMx` [@Neale-Hunter-Pritikin-etal-2016] fits the same state space model
with its own Kalman filter (`OpenMx::mxExpectationStateSpace()`; @Hunter-2018).
Its matrices have the names used in engineering:
`A` is the transition matrix $\boldsymbol{\beta}$,
`B` holds the intercepts of the dynamic model,
`C` is the loading matrix $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$,
`D` holds the intercepts of the measurement model,
`Q` is the process noise covariance matrix,
and `R` is the measurement error covariance matrix.
The parameter labels are the dynr names;
as in dynr, a label used in two places is one shared parameter,
and the starting values are the population values.

Two details differ from dynr.
First, OpenMx reads the data as a single time series.
To start the filter again at the first occasion of every individual,
each individual gets a group,
and all groups use the matrices of one parent model,
so every individual has the same parameters.
Second, OpenMx starts the filter one occasion before the first row,
so the first row has the state mean $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}_{0} + \mathbf{B} \mathbf{u}$
and the state covariance $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{P}_{0} \mathbf{A}^{\prime} + \mathbf{Q}$,
with the constant input $\mathbf{u} = 1$.
Setting
$\mathbf{x}_{0} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}_{0} - \mathbf{B} \mathbf{u} \right)$
and
$\mathbf{P}_{0} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \left( \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} - \mathbf{Q} \right) \left( \mathbf{A}^{-1} \right)^{\prime}$
gives the first occasion the initial condition of the model,
so the likelihood is the same as in dynr.
This needs an invertible $\mathbf{A}$, which holds here.

The two helper functions below are the same in every vignette of the package.
`MxMat()` makes an OpenMx matrix from values and dynr-style labels
(`"fixed"` marks a fixed element),
and `FitMxSSM()` builds the groups and fits the model.


``` r
MxMat <- function(values, labels, name) {
  values <- as.matrix(values)
  labels <- matrix(
    data = labels,
    nrow = nrow(values),
    ncol = ncol(values)
  )
  free <- labels != "fixed"
  labels[!free] <- NA
  OpenMx::mxMatrix(
    type = "Full",
    values = values,
    free = free,
    labels = labels,
    name = name
  )
}
FitMxSSM <- function(data, observed, matrices, name) {
  # the groups refer to the matrices of the parent model
  shared <- function(x) {
    paste0(name, ".", x)
  }
  expectation <- OpenMx::mxExpectationStateSpace(
    A = shared("A"),
    B = shared("B"),
    C = shared("C"),
    D = shared("D"),
    Q = shared("Q"),
    R = shared("R"),
    x0 = shared("x0"),
    P0 = shared("P0"),
    u = shared("u")
  )
  # OpenMx needs the names of the observed variables and of the states on C
  for (i in seq_along(matrices)) {
    if (matrices[[i]]$name == "C") {
      dimnames(matrices[[i]]) <- list(
        observed,
        paste0("eta_", seq_len(ncol(matrices[[i]]$values)))
      )
    }
  }
  persons <- split(
    x = data[, observed, drop = FALSE],
    f = data[, "id"]
  )
  groups <- paste0("id_", names(persons))
  submodels <- lapply(
    X = seq_along(persons),
    FUN = function(i) {
      OpenMx::mxModel(
        name = groups[i],
        expectation,
        OpenMx::mxFitFunctionML(),
        OpenMx::mxData(
          observed = persons[[i]],
          type = "raw"
        )
      )
    }
  )
  model <- OpenMx::mxModel(
    name = name,
    matrices,
    OpenMx::mxMatrix(
      type = "Unit",
      nrow = 1,
      ncol = 1,
      name = "u"
    ),
    # the first occasion gets the initial condition of the model
    OpenMx::mxAlgebra(
      expression = solve(A) %*% (mu0 - B %*% u),
      name = "x0"
    ),
    OpenMx::mxAlgebra(
      expression = solve(A) %*% (sigma0 - Q) %*% t(solve(A)),
      name = "P0"
    ),
    submodels,
    OpenMx::mxFitFunctionMultigroup(groups = groups)
  )
  # retries from perturbed starting values only if the first run fails
  OpenMx::mxTryHard(
    model = model,
    extraTries = 5,
    silent = TRUE
  )
}
```

The matrices of the model, with the dynr labels.
The transition matrix is a fixed part
(each level carries over and adds its slope)
plus the self-feedback and coupling effects,
so `A` is an algebra, the sum of the two.
There is no process noise (`Q` is zero).


``` r
feedback <- matrix(data = 0, nrow = 4, ncol = 4)
feedback[1:2, 1:2] <- c(b_1, g_2_1, g_1_2, b_2)
labels_feedback <- matrix(data = "fixed", nrow = 4, ncol = 4)
labels_feedback[1:2, 1:2] <- c("b_1", "g_2_1", "g_1_2", "b_2")
labels_sigma0 <- matrix(
  data = c(
    "sigma0_1_1", "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_3_1", "sigma0_4_1",
    "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_2_2", "sigma0_3_2", "sigma0_4_2",
    "sigma0_3_1", "sigma0_3_2", "sigma0_3_3", "sigma0_4_3",
    "sigma0_4_1", "sigma0_4_2", "sigma0_4_3", "sigma0_4_4"
  ),
  nrow = 4
)
mx_matrices <- list(
  MxMat(values = beta - feedback, labels = "fixed", name = "carry"),
  MxMat(values = feedback, labels = labels_feedback, name = "feedback"),
  OpenMx::mxAlgebra(expression = carry + feedback, name = "A"),
  MxMat(values = alpha, labels = "fixed", name = "B"),
  MxMat(values = lambda, labels = "fixed", name = "C"),
  MxMat(values = nu, labels = "fixed", name = "D"),
  MxMat(values = psi, labels = "fixed", name = "Q"),
  MxMat(
    values = theta,
    labels = c("theta_1_1", "fixed", "fixed", "theta_2_2"),
    name = "R"
  ),
  MxMat(
    values = mu0,
    labels = c("mu0_1_1", "mu0_2_1", "mu0_3_1", "mu0_4_1"),
    name = "mu0"
  ),
  MxMat(values = sigma0, labels = labels_sigma0, name = "sigma0")
)
```


``` r
fit_mx_ssm <- FitMxSSM(
  data = data,
  observed = c("y1", "y2"),
  matrices = mx_matrices,
  name = "lcs"
)
```

### lavaan: Structural Equation Model

The same model in SEM form, fitted with `lavaan`,
should give nearly the same estimates.
In SEM, each variable at each occasion is a separate observed variable
in one row per individual (wide format).
Each observed score has a true-level factor;
each true level after the first is the previous true level
plus a change factor;
and each change factor is the slope
plus the self-feedback and coupling effects.

#### Wide Data Set

`as.data.frame()` with `long = FALSE` returns the data in wide format.


``` r
data_wide <- as.data.frame(sim, long = FALSE)
head(data_wide)
```

#### Model

The model has the same structure for every occasion,
so we write it with `paste0()`.
The parameter labels match the dynr names.
Giving the self-feedback and coupling effects
and the measurement error variances the same label on every occasion
constrains them to be equal over time,
as in the state space model.


``` r
waves <- 0:(time - 1)
now <- waves[-1]
before <- waves[-time]
model <- paste(
  c(
    "# true levels",
    paste0("l1_", waves, " =~ 1 * y1_", waves),
    paste0("l2_", waves, " =~ 1 * y2_", waves),
    "# each true level is the previous level plus the change",
    paste0("l1_", now, " ~ 1 * l1_", before),
    paste0("l2_", now, " ~ 1 * l2_", before),
    paste0("l1_", now, " ~~ 0 * l1_", now),
    paste0("l2_", now, " ~~ 0 * l2_", now),
    paste0("d1_", now, " =~ 1 * l1_", now),
    paste0("d2_", now, " =~ 1 * l2_", now),
    "# the change: self-feedback and coupling",
    paste0("d1_", now, " ~ b_1 * l1_", before, " + g_1_2 * l2_", before),
    paste0("d2_", now, " ~ b_2 * l2_", before, " + g_2_1 * l1_", before),
    paste0("d1_", now, " ~~ 0 * d1_", now),
    paste0("d2_", now, " ~~ 0 * d2_", now),
    "# the change: slopes",
    paste0("s1 =~ ", paste0("1 * d1_", now, collapse = " + ")),
    paste0("s2 =~ ", paste0("1 * d2_", now, collapse = " + ")),
    "# initial true levels and slopes: means",
    "l1_0 ~ mu0_1_1 * 1",
    "l2_0 ~ mu0_2_1 * 1",
    "s1 ~ mu0_3_1 * 1",
    "s2 ~ mu0_4_1 * 1",
    "# initial true levels and slopes: variances and covariances",
    "l1_0 ~~ sigma0_1_1 * l1_0",
    "l2_0 ~~ sigma0_2_2 * l2_0",
    "s1 ~~ sigma0_3_3 * s1",
    "s2 ~~ sigma0_4_4 * s2",
    "l1_0 ~~ sigma0_2_1 * l2_0",
    "l1_0 ~~ sigma0_3_1 * s1",
    "l1_0 ~~ sigma0_4_1 * s2",
    "l2_0 ~~ sigma0_3_2 * s1",
    "l2_0 ~~ sigma0_4_2 * s2",
    "s1 ~~ sigma0_4_3 * s2",
    "# measurement error variances, equal over time; no observed intercepts",
    paste0("y1_", waves, " ~~ theta_1_1 * y1_", waves),
    paste0("y2_", waves, " ~~ theta_2_2 * y2_", waves),
    paste0("y1_", waves, " ~ 0 * 1"),
    paste0("y2_", waves, " ~ 0 * 1")
  ),
  collapse = "\n"
)
cat(model)
#> # true levels
#> l1_0 =~ 1 * y1_0
#> l1_1 =~ 1 * y1_1
#> l1_2 =~ 1 * y1_2
#> l1_3 =~ 1 * y1_3
```

`lavaan::lavaan()` adds nothing to the model by itself,
so every parameter above is exactly the one written.


``` r

  model = model,
  data = data_wide
)
```

### OpenMx: Structural Equation Model

The same SEM in `OpenMx`, written with `OpenMx::mxPath()`
on the wide data.
One-headed arrows are loadings and regressions,
two-headed arrows are variances and covariances,
and arrows from `"one"` are means.
A path that is not written is fixed at zero,
so the zero residual variances, covariances, and intercepts
of the lavaan model need no lines here.
The labels are the dynr names,
and the starting values are the population values.

`connect = "unique.pairs"` adds every variance and covariance
among the initial true levels and the slopes;
their labels and values are the lower triangle of the label matrix
and of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}$, in the same order.


``` r
waves <- 0:(time - 1)
y1 <- paste0("y1_", waves)
y2 <- paste0("y2_", waves)
l1 <- paste0("l1_", waves)
l2 <- paste0("l2_", waves)
d1 <- paste0("d1_", waves[-1])
d2 <- paste0("d2_", waves[-1])
initial <- c("l1_0", "l2_0", "s1", "s2")
mx_sem <- OpenMx::mxModel(
  name = "lcs_sem",
  type = "RAM",
  manifestVars = c(y1, y2),
  latentVars = c(l1, l2, d1, d2, "s1", "s2"),
  OpenMx::mxData(observed = data_wide[, c(y1, y2)], type = "raw"),
  # true levels
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = l1, to = y1, free = FALSE, values = 1),
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = l2, to = y2, free = FALSE, values = 1),
  # each true level is the previous level plus the change
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = l1[-time], to = l1[-1], free = FALSE, values = 1),
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = l2[-time], to = l2[-1], free = FALSE, values = 1),
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = d1, to = l1[-1], free = FALSE, values = 1),
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = d2, to = l2[-1], free = FALSE, values = 1),
  # the change: self-feedback and coupling
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = l1[-time], to = d1, labels = "b_1", values = b_1),
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = l2[-time], to = d1, labels = "g_1_2", values = g_1_2),
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = l2[-time], to = d2, labels = "b_2", values = b_2),
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = l1[-time], to = d2, labels = "g_2_1", values = g_2_1),
  # the change: slopes
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = "s1", to = d1, free = FALSE, values = 1),
  OpenMx::mxPath(from = "s2", to = d2, free = FALSE, values = 1),
  # initial true levels and slopes: means
  OpenMx::mxPath(
    from = "one",
    to = initial,
    labels = c("mu0_1_1", "mu0_2_1", "mu0_3_1", "mu0_4_1"),
    values = mu0
  ),
  # initial true levels and slopes: variances and covariances
  OpenMx::mxPath(
    from = initial,
    arrows = 2,
    connect = "unique.pairs",
    labels = labels_sigma0[lower.tri(labels_sigma0, diag = TRUE)],
    values = sigma0[lower.tri(sigma0, diag = TRUE)]
  ),
  # measurement error variances, equal over time
  OpenMx::mxPath(
    from = y1, arrows = 2, labels = "theta_1_1", values = theta[1, 1]
  ),
  OpenMx::mxPath(
    from = y2, arrows = 2, labels = "theta_2_2", values = theta[2, 2]
  )
)
```


``` r
fit_mx_sem <- OpenMx::mxRun(
  model = mx_sem,
  silent = TRUE
)
summary(fit_mx_sem)
```

## Population Values and Estimates

Each table below puts the population values used to simulate the data
next to the estimates of one method.
Bias is the estimate minus the population value.
Because each model is fitted to a single simulated data set,
this is the error of one estimate, not a Monte Carlo bias,
which would average over many replications.
The 95% confidence interval is the Wald interval,
$\hat{\theta} \pm 1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}$,
unless the caption says otherwise,
and `Covers` shows whether it contains the population value.
The parameter names are the dynr names in every table.


``` r
EstimatesTable <- function(population, estimate, se, ll = NULL, ul = NULL) {
  z <- stats::qnorm(p = 0.975)
  if (is.null(ll)) {
    ll <- estimate - z * se
  }
  if (is.null(ul)) {
    ul <- estimate + z * se
  }
  data.frame(
    Parameter = names(population),
    Population = unname(population),
    Estimate = unname(estimate),
    SE = unname(se),
    Bias = unname(estimate - population),
    `2.5%` = unname(ll),
    `97.5%` = unname(ul),
    Covers = unname(population >= ll & population <= ul),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}
```


``` r
population <- c(
  mu0_1_1 = mu0[1],
  mu0_2_1 = mu0[2],
  mu0_3_1 = mu0[3],
  mu0_4_1 = mu0[4],
  sigma0_1_1 = sigma0[1, 1],
  sigma0_2_1 = sigma0[2, 1],
  sigma0_3_1 = sigma0[3, 1],
  sigma0_4_1 = sigma0[4, 1],
  sigma0_2_2 = sigma0[2, 2],
  sigma0_3_2 = sigma0[3, 2],
  sigma0_4_2 = sigma0[4, 2],
  sigma0_3_3 = sigma0[3, 3],
  sigma0_4_3 = sigma0[4, 3],
  sigma0_4_4 = sigma0[4, 4],
  b_1 = b_1,
  b_2 = b_2,
  g_1_2 = g_1_2,
  g_2_1 = g_2_1,
  theta_1_1 = theta[1, 1],
  theta_2_2 = theta[2, 2]
)
```

### dynr


``` r
dynr_est <- coef(results)
dynr_se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(results)))
knitr::kable(
  x = EstimatesTable(
    population = population,
    estimate = dynr_est[names(population)],
    se = dynr_se[names(population)]
  ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Population values and dynr estimates (one simulated data set)"
)
```

### All Methods

The estimates of every method side by side.
The methods maximize the same likelihood,
so their estimates should agree closely.


``` r
knitr::kable(
  x = data.frame(
    Parameter = names(population),
    Population = unname(population),
    `dynr` = unname(dynr_est[names(population)]),
    `OpenMx (SSM)` = unname(mx_ssm_est[names(population)]),
    `lavaan` = unname(lavaan_est[names(population)]),
    `OpenMx (SEM)` = unname(mx_sem_est[names(population)]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Population values and the estimates of every method"
)
```
